tldr: OSWORLD is the first scalable, real computer environment for benchmarking multimodal agents on open-ended tasks across Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, with 369 real-world tasks that expose significant gaps between human performance (72.36%) and the best model (12.24%).
contributions: Introduction of OSWORLD, a scalable real computer environment supporting task setup, execution-based evaluation, and interactive learning across multiple operating systems

A benchmark of 369 real-world computer tasks involving web/desktop apps, OS file I/O, and multi-application workflows, each with initial state setup configurations and custom execution-based evaluation scripts
Extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLM/VLM-based agents revealing significant deficiencies in their ability to serve as computer assistants
methods: The authors built OSWORLD as a virtual machine-based environment that supports free-form keyboard and mouse control of real applications across Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS. They created a benchmark of 369 tasks derived from real-world sources including forums, tutorials, and guidelines, each annotated with initial state setup configurations and custom execution-based evaluation scripts. Tasks span single-app interactions and multi-application workflows involving Chrome, VLC, Thunderbird, VS Code, LibreOffice, GIMP, and basic OS apps. They evaluated multiple agent baselines including GPT-4V series, Gemini series, Claude-3 Opus, Qwen-Max, Mixtral, Llama-3, and CogAgent.
results: Humans accomplish over 72.36% of tasks while the best model achieves only 12.24%, with some application subsets reaching 0%. For multi-app workflow tasks, the highest baseline performance is only 6.57%. The benchmark includes 134 unique evaluation functions. Adding accessibility trees and Set-of-Mark can help but may also cause misguidance. Feeding higher resolution and more trajectory history can double performance but requires longer context length.
limitations: VLM-based agents struggle with GUI grounding (predicting precise coordinates from screenshots), tend to produce repetitive actions, cannot handle noise from unexpected application windows, and have limited knowledge of basic GUI interactions and domain-specific app features. The benchmark creation was labor-intensive, requiring 9 computer science students over 3 months and approximately 1800 man-hours. Some tasks have real-time characteristics that require dynamic evaluation functions.
